newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgium receives Renault news with dismay.
newsitem.headline: Belgium receives Renault news with dismay.

text.p: Belgium received French car maker Renault's confirmation of plans to close a factory near Brussels with a mixture of dismay and resignation on Sunday, although some condemned workers vowed to continue to fight.

Flying in the face of union and political opposition both at home and abroad, the French car maker on Saturday confirmed plans first announced in February to close the Vilvoorde plant before the end of the year.

Belgian Prime Minister Jean-Luc Dehaene, who lives in the town, had harsh words for his French counterpart Lionel Jospin, who pledged during France's recent electoral campaign to review Renault's decision. The French state owns 46 percent of Renault.
Dehaene appeared however to rule out further intervention, telling VTM television news the Belgian government had done "the maximum" it could to keep the plant open.
Everything must now be done to get Renault Industrie Belgique's 3,100 workers the best redundancy deal possible and find new work for the town, Dehaene said.

Talks had been held with Japanese car maker Toyota about locating a new assembly plant in Belgium, but even if these were successful they would not provide any near term solution to Vilvoorde's plight, he said.
Belgian unions said Renault staff would assemble on Monday morning to consider what steps to take next. There were already signs some were not prepared to simply negotiate a settlement.

"The occupation of the factory and the strike will likely continue at Vilvoorde and there could be much tougher action than those we have seen up to now," union leader Karel Gacoms told Belgium's Belga news agency on Saturday.
Renault Industrie Belgique works council chairman Herman Smeulders said unions wanted Renault to keep the factory open until next year while staff looked for new work, Belga reported.
Speaking at the factory on Sunday, he also branded insufficient an offer made by the company to employ around 400 staff over the next three years in unspecified industrial work.
Renault workers have been occupying the factory since the closure plan was announced on February 27. They still hold a "war chest" of semi-finished Megane cars worth millions of francs.
